tours.title: Foundations to Transformers
tours.summary: Follow a small set of landmarks from formal computation to the architecture behind modern language models.

steps.narration: Turing's abstract universal machine established a formal model of computation that still describes most digital AI software.
The 1956 Dartmouth workshop gave artificial intelligence its name and an enduring, if overoptimistic, founding agenda.
Rosenblatt's perceptron learned from examples and became an early emblem of both neural-network promise and hype.
Backpropagation made multilayer credit assignment practical and became a central training method of the modern neural era.
ImageNet paired a very large labeled image collection with an annual contest, making deep-learning progress easier to measure.
AlexNet combined GPU training and convolutional networks to produce the ImageNet result that accelerated deep learning's adoption.
The Transformer centered attention and parallel training, supplying the architecture that defines much of the current era.

tours.title: Two Winters and Revivals
tours.summary: Trace the field's early optimism, funding contractions, expert-system boom and collapse, and neural revival.

steps.narration: Dartmouth's founders gave the field a bold name and timetable, establishing expectations that proved much harder to meet.
The perceptron demonstrated learning from examples while public promises ran well ahead of the machine's actual capabilities.
Minsky and Papert documented limits of single-layer perceptrons; the broader funding reaction also sidelined multilayer approaches.
The Lighthill review criticized unmet AI promises and contributed to a long contraction in British research support.
Expert-system shells turned hand-built rules and knowledge engineering into a substantial commercial industry.
The expert-system and Lisp-machine markets collapsed, making the AI label commercially toxic for another period.
Effective multilayer credit assignment helped restore connectionist research and prepared the ground for later deep learning.

tours.title: The Scaling Era
tours.summary: Connect the compute, data, architecture, and empirical scaling milestones behind frontier language models.

steps.narration: Decades of rising transistor counts supplied an underlying compute trend for successive waves of AI research.
General-purpose GPU computing turned graphics hardware into a practical engine for large neural-network workloads.
ImageNet supplied both labeled data and a visible benchmark through which deep-learning systems could be compared.
AlexNet's 2012 ImageNet result demonstrated the combined value of GPUs, data, and deep convolutional models.
Attention-based parallelism made the Transformer especially compatible with increasingly large training runs.
Empirical scaling laws related model loss to compute, data, and parameter budgets, while Chinchilla revised their balance.
GPT-3 showed much stronger few-shot behavior at 175 billion parameters and accelerated the language-model API era.
The map's frontier grouping tracks assistants combining reasoning, multimodality, and agent capabilities while competing on reliability and cost.

tours.title: Reinforcement Learning Keeps Returning
tours.summary: See how sequential decision theory, value learning, policy optimization, self-play, and preferences recur across AI eras.

steps.narration: Markov decision processes and Bellman equations provided a mathematical framework for sequential decisions under uncertainty.
Q-learning established off-policy value learning with convergence guarantees in the tabular setting.
Policy-gradient methods optimized actions directly and helped establish the actor-critic family used in later systems.
TD-Gammon combined a neural network, temporal-difference learning, and self-play to reach top-level backgammon.
DQN joined deep networks, Q-learning, and experience replay to learn Atari games directly from pixels.
AlphaGo combined policy and value networks with tree search and self-play to defeat Lee Sedol.
RLHF made learned human preferences one component of instruction-following assistants, while retaining specification risks.
Tool-using language-model agents extend models from generating text to acting, with reliability still a central limitation.

tours.title: The Diffusion Decade
tours.summary: Follow modern generative modeling from latent-variable and adversarial systems to diffusion across media and language.

steps.narration: Variational autoencoders introduced probabilistic latent spaces that could be sampled and optimized with neural networks.
GANs used adversarial training to dominate much of image generation before diffusion became the more stable workhorse.
Diffusion systems learn to reverse a noising process and now support generation across several data modalities.
Latent diffusion and classifier-free guidance made high-resolution, language-directed image generation broadly practical.
Diffusion Transformers apply scalable Transformer backbones to diffusion models in image, video, and audio work.
Diffusion language models explore parallel denoising as an early alternative to left-to-right generation.

tours.title: Agents and Alignment
tours.summary: Trace selected approaches to aligning and evaluating increasingly capable tool-using agents without implying that the problem is solved.

steps.narration: Early agent-foundations work pursued decision-theoretic alignment for hypothetical superintelligence before the LLM era.
RLHF uses human comparisons to train reward models, alongside supervised tuning, data curation, and other safety measures.
Constitutional AI has models critique outputs against written principles as one way to scale oversight beyond direct labeling.
Language-model agents can call tools and act in external environments, expanding both usefulness and reliability concerns.
Interactive benchmarks test agents in websites, repositories, and computers, exposing failures that static question answering misses.
AI control research studies monitors, resampling, editing, and limited audits as defenses against intentionally subversive models.
Self-generating agents create tasks, skills, or modifications, but reported gains remain bounded by their environments and verifiers.
Provable agent boundaries is a proposed research direction for testable containment, permissions, and corrigibility guarantees.
